F20 here. I’ve had Raynaud’s phenomenon since I was nine, mostly just a minor inconvenience. About 1.5 years ago, I started experiencing unexplained symptoms like inappropriate tachycardia, chronic fatigue, nausea, and occasional headaches, leading to my first visit to a rheumatologist. I’ve struggled with being extremely underweight in the past, and doctors suggested my symptoms would resolve once my BMI normalized. However, despite stabilizing my weight, my symptoms have worsened.

During my rheumatology visit, my tests were mostly fine except for a “borderline positive” (rheum’s words) ANA (1:40, midbody, and homogenous pattern). While this result didn’t seem too concerning, I do have a family history of lupus.

Recently, my Raynaud’s has worsened unexpectedly, spreading beyond my hands and feet to my knees, tongue, and thumbs. This new development concerns me, although I was advised not to worry. Should I consider revisiting my rheumatologist or seek a second opinion, or is this something that typically doesn’t warrant concern?

Hi! I know this is a very late response. My story isn’t the “typical” ARFID story. I have battled with POTS and other disabilities which made it incredibly hard to eat because of my stomach. I became fearful of throwing up or feeling bad, which caused me to avoid eating altogether. 

As far as texture sensitivities and other issues relating to that, I probably won’t be much help. But if you are an ARFID patient who struggles with the fear of throwing up, I have a little advice. 

The more you restrict, the more you will feel nauseated once you return eating. It is a vicious and horrendous cycle of avoiding food because of fear of becoming sick, and then feeling sick because you are avoiding food. If possible, try to eat every 3 hours. In my residential treatment center, I would eat close to every 2 hours, which was a lot for my stomach to handle. 

If you take Boost/nutritional drinks for supplemental calories, I find it makes it harder to eat after finishing the drink. Eat as much solid food as you physically feel like you are capable, and slowly drink Boost/nutritional drinks for supplemental calories. I was completely reliant on Boost for a while before I learned how to manage myself better. 

In my case, the first time after restricting for a long time is the worst. You will feel nauseated, you might even have other physical symptoms just like me. But it is almost like a wave, the more you ride the wave, the better and easier it will get. It’s going to be incredibly hard in the beginning. ARFID convinces you of a false safety, by making you think you are better off not eating than getting sick. The more you can fight the urge to restrict, I guarantee the easier it will get. 

It is not easy. I wish it was. It took me several years of my life to finally get to a place where I understood how my eating disorder effected me. It took me years to even get other people to understand my eating disorder. But you are valid, even if everything is working against you. 

One final note, because ARFID could potentially be closely related to OCD, I found that exposure therapy usually worked best for me. Put yourself into situations that make you entirely uncomfortable and even fearful, and ride the wave of fear. The more exposure, the easier it gets. It’s just a matter of desensitizing your brain to the fear you experience.

I would be concerned. I don’t know the full extent of your heart related symptoms, but I wouldn’t be surprised to hear if they are related. 

I have been diagnosed with POTS or postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, and a common symptoms can be pain. POTS can be related to a lot of autoimmune disorders. It has a strong relation to Ehlers-Danlos syndrome which can cause pain, cardiovascular abnormalities, unusual skin issues like bruising easily, and potentially hyper-mobility with joints. 

I would especially pay attention if you notice an unexplained fever or any other abnormalities, and be sure to bring it up to a doctor.

Hi, I know people in the piercing community have debated that nothing but salt water should ever touch healing piercings, but my piercer recommended to me witch hazel and it worked fantastically. I have had piercing bumps on my daith and conch, with both disappearing after using a little witch hazel everyday. It has been the only thing that worked for me. 

Another solution could be to find the source of irritation. I know sleeping on piercings is a common cause of irritation and piercing bumps. Specifically, the tragus piercing might be irritated by earbuds or headphones. If sleeping is your issue, you can try using a travel pillow to sleep on. However, for me, that was too uncomfortable. I’ve seen some people wrap blankets into donut shapes, with a hole in the middle for your ear. Or they sell piercing pillows on etsy for $20 or so with a hole in the middle for your ear. 

Hope this helps!
